candidates.title: A toxic relationship in Math!| Definition of limits| epsilon- delta| A Math stand- up! #mathtalk
candidates.description: I hope they find peace soon. 😭 Till then… do you think I should do a whole series covering more of these epsilon–delta proofs? 👀 Because even with all this fun context, epsilon and delta are genuinely a mathematician’s best friends. 💛 Why? Because they give us a precise language to talk about ideas that otherwise feel almost impossible to pin down. Take a limit. We casually say, “as x gets closer and closer to a, f(x) gets closer and closer to L.” But what does “closer and closer” actually mean? How close is close enough? How do we quantify that closeness? And how can we turn an intuitive statement into something we can actually prove? That’s where ε (epsilon) and δ (delta) enter. For every tiny tolerance ε that we choose for the output, we can find a corresponding δ that tells us how close x needs to be to a. And suddenly, this vague idea of “approaching” becomes a mathematically precise statement. That is the beauty of the epsilon–delta definition of a limit — it teaches us how mathematics turns intuition into rigor. And honestly… this is one of the moments where calculus starts becoming real analysis. 🥹 So yes, epsilon and delta may be having their own little marital crisis here… …but mathematically? Best friends. candidates.title: What If Your Money Gets Stuck Together in the ATM? #howitworks #explained
candidates.description: What if your money gets stuck together in the ATM? Two twenties stuck together: do you get a free $20? No. Inside many ATMs, every bill rolls between two steel rollers. One bill lifts the top roller a hair, and the machine measures it. Two stuck bills are twice as thick, so they lift it twice as far. A gate flips the pair into a hidden reject bin, the machine picks one fresh bill, and you get exactly what you asked for. Would you have kept the extra twenty? Tell us in the comments. What we simplified: • ATMs differ. We show one patented design (NCR): a thickness gauge between steel rollers and a gate into a reject bin. A Diebold design gauges the bills the same way but runs the rollers backward to push a double back into the stack. • The roller's lift is exaggerated so you can see it. A bill is about a tenth of a millimeter thick, and the gauge in one NCR patent senses movements as small as 5 microns. • The dial with 1, 2 and 3 is a picture of the machine's reading. The patent compares the reading with ranges for one, two and three notes. • What happens to rejected bills after that is not shown. The patents say only that they go into the reject bin and the count is recorded. Where the facts come from: • NCR patent US5988634 (thickness gauge, doubles diverted to the reject bin): https://patents.google.com/patent/US5988634A/en • NCR patent US7296735 (5-micron sensing, multiples never sent to the exit): https://patents.google.com/patent/US7296735B2/en • Diebold patent US4494747 (friction picking, one note per cycle, doubles pushed back): https://patents.google.com/patent/US4494747A/en • Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta working paper 2019-2 ("most ATMs in the United States dispense multiples of $20 bills"): https://ideas.repec.org/p/fip/fedawp/2019-02.html Made by Kettlo. Idea and direction: Tarek Script and research: every claim above is checked against the sources listed. Animation: built shot by shot in code, in 3D. No stock footage, no templates. Music and sound effects: original, made for this video. Narration: produced with ElevenLabs and directed line by line. #atm #howitworks #money #engineering #machines #money #whatif #explained

candidates.title: these spinning circles are drawing a dotted sixteenth note 🎵
candidates.description: The outline of a dotted sixteenth note, sampled at 2048 points, is a sum of spinning circles: z(t) = ∑ cₖ eⁱᵏᵗ, with the cₖ from its discrete Fourier transform. Circle k has radius |cₖ| and turns k times per lap. Keep only the N biggest circles and the widest gap to the outline is 27.9% of the symbol's height at N = 2, 9.0% at N = 8, 2.7% at N = 32, 0.58% at N = 128 and 0.14% at N = 512. The dot is a separate shape, so the circles draw the note as one continuous line and hop across to the dot and back: the short straight stroke near the notehead is that hop. The sound is built the same way: an A that gains overtones every time more circles join, with more plucked notes each stage. You asked for a dotted sixteenth (and a semiquaver) in the comments, so here it is. candidates.title: How your brain builds a memory, step by step
candidates.description: You're the designer of your brain's memory system. Every fix creates the next problem: a fleeting snapshot (sensory memory), a filter (attention), a small workspace that holds about four chunks (working memory), grouping (chunking), a lasting store (long-term memory), sleep that strengthens new memories (consolidation), cues to find them again (retrieval), and review spread over time (spaced repetition). A simplified model, not the whole story. Sources: Sperling (1960), Psychological Monographs 74(11). Cowan (2001), Behavioral and Brain Sciences 24(1), 87-114. Miller (1956), Psychological Review 63(2), 81-97. Diekelmann & Born (2010), Nature Reviews Neuroscience 11, 114-126. Tulving & Thomson (1973), Psychological Review 80(5), 352-373. candidates.title: Your Brain Deletes Memories on Purpose - and That's One of the Smartest Things It Does
candidates.description: Every night while you sleep, your brain runs a compression pass. It doesn't store everything. It decides. What was significant? What was a pattern? What can safely go? This isn't a malfunction. It's an active, deliberate process — and it's one of the most sophisticated things your brain does. A brain that stored everything equally would have no way to tell what mattered. No hierarchy. No signal. Just an equal weight of every moment you've ever lived — the coffee, the crisis, the conversation — all carrying the same vividness, the same presence. Forgetting is how the brain assigns significance. What stays, stayed for a reason. What fades, faded so something else could be clear. The brain that deletes is building meaning. Not losing it. #memory #forgetting #brainscience #neuroscience #psychology #cognition #science #mentalhealth #stillrunning #shorts #shortvideo

candidates.title: Why 0.999... Is Mathematically Equal to 1
candidates.description: 0.999... is not "almost 1" — it is literally another way of writing the exact number 1. This 10-second visual explainer breaks down why the repeating decimal 0.999... equals 1 using a single 1×1 unit square and four classic mathematical proofs: The Fraction Proof: 1/3 = 0.333..., so multiplying both sides by 3 gives 3/3 = 0.999... = 1. The Algebraic Proof: Setting x = 0.999... and subtracting it from 10x = 9.999... leaves 9x = 9, so x = 1. The Infinite Geometric Series: Adding 0.9 + 0.09 + 0.009 + ... fills the entire unit square with zero leftover space. The Number Line: Between any two distinct real numbers, you can always fit another number. Because 1 − 0.999... = 0, no number exists between them. Key insight: Our intuition trips up because we expect every real number to have only one decimal representation. In reality, any terminating decimal (like 1 or 0.5) can also be written as an infinite repeating 9s decimal (0.999... or 0.4999...). Save this Short as a quick reference for calculus, real analysis, or the next time this math debate comes up. #Mathematics #0999Equals1 #MathExplained

candidates.title: 5 Photography Tips for Beginners
candidates.description: “Thinking about getting into photography? Yesterday I was talking with a young woman who wanted to learn, and I shared a few things I wish someone had told me when I was starting out. Here are five tips you can try this week. One. Learn what your camera settings actually do. Shutter speed freezes motion, aperture changes how much of the scene is sharp, and ISO can help when the light is low. Change one setting at a time and see what happens. Two. Look at the light before you take the picture. Photograph the same thing in direct sun, in open shade, and beside a window. You’ll see how much the light changes the mood. Three. Give yourself a place to learn. I told her to check out Kelby training for lessons on camera basics and Photoshop. Pick one lesson, then go try it with your own photos. Four. Get to know Adobe Camera Raw. Start with exposure and white balance. Take a picture that looks a little too dark or too yellow and see what two small adjustments can do. Five. Learn Levels in Photoshop. Start by adjusting the shadows, midtones, and highlights. Then try the individual red, green, and blue channels to see how Levels can help correct a color cast. And here’s your assignment. Pick something you see every day and photograph it three different ways. A coffee mug will do just fine. It’s amazing what you start to notice when you give yourself a reason to look.” Carol Brightbill Photographer & Graphic Designer www.carolbrightbill.com

candidates.title: This Broken Bone Created Humanity! 🦴😱#shorts
candidates.description: This Broken Bone Created Humanity! 🦴😱#shorts Did you know the first true sign of human civilization wasn't a spear, a stone wheel, or a clay pot—it was a healed leg bone? 🦴🏛️ In this 2D minimalist stickman documentary, we reveal one of the most shocking discoveries in prehistoric anthropology: The Healed Femur Paradox (inspired by anthropologist Margaret Mead). In the brutal prehistoric wild, a fractured femur was a guaranteed death sentence. An injured hominin couldn't run to water, couldn't forage, and couldn't escape predators. A human thigh bone takes at least six to eight weeks of absolute rest to heal properly. Yet, fossil records dating back over 15,000 years reveal ancient skeletons with fully mended femurs. That means someone dragged that injured hunter to safety. Someone carried them water across dry savannas, shared valuable food, and stood guard against night predators for two whole months until they could walk again. Humanity didn't conquer the wild with sharper claws or brute force—compassion and caring for the wounded became our greatest survival superpower. 🤝❤️ Would early humans have survived without empathy? Share your thoughts below! 👇💬 🔔 Subscribe to @Stickverse for weekly 2D stickman animations breaking down prehistoric human evolution, ancient survival secrets, and untold anthropology mysteries! 🏹 #ancienthumans #humanevolution #paleoanthropology #prehistory #ancientcivilization #humanorigins #stickverse #sciencefacts #prehistoricsurvival #anthropology

candidates.title: Riemann Sum vs Integration Explained Visually | Area Under the Sine Curve #riemann #integration
candidates.description: Explore the beautiful connection between Riemann sums and definite integration through this engaging mathematical visualization of the sine function. This video demonstrates how the concept of summation gradually transforms into the idea of integration by using rectangles to approximate the area under the curve of y = sin(x) from zero to pi. Discover how the Riemann sum method works by dividing the area beneath a continuous curve into smaller rectangular sections. Each rectangle represents an approximate contribution to the total area, and the sum of these individual areas provides an estimate of the definite integral. As the number of rectangles increases, the width of each rectangle decreases, producing a more accurate approximation of the actual area. This mathematical visualization illustrates the fundamental relationship between finite sums, limits, and calculus. Watch how the number of rectangles increases progressively, making the rectangular approximation approach the smooth region beneath the sine curve. The comparison between the numerical Riemann sum and the exact value of the definite integral highlights one of the most important ideas in mathematical analysis. The definite integral of sin(x) over the interval from zero to pi equals 2. This result provides a clear example of how integration calculates the accumulated area under a function and how numerical approximation methods can approach an exact mathematical result. The visualization also introduces the midpoint Riemann sum, a numerical integration technique that uses the midpoint of each subinterval to determine the height of its corresponding rectangle. This video is ideal for students learning calculus, definite integrals, limits, numerical integration, and the mathematical foundations of area calculation. It helps make abstract mathematical concepts more intuitive by connecting graphical representations with numerical approximations and analytical results. Key mathematical concepts explored in this video include Riemann sums, definite integration, the sine function, area under a curve, midpoint approximation, limits, continuous functions, and the relationship between summation and integration. These concepts form an essential foundation for advanced calculus, mathematical modeling, physics, engineering, numerical analysis, and other scientific applications. For students preparing for mathematics examinations, competitive exams, or higher-level calculus courses, this visual explanation offers an accessible way to understand how integration emerges from the process of adding increasingly smaller contributions. Mathematics teachers can also use this example to demonstrate the connection between geometric area, numerical approximation, and exact integration. The clean visual presentation, continuously changing rectangles, and live numerical comparison make this mathematics video suitable for YouTube Shorts and other short-form educational content. It combines mathematical intuition with visual learning to make calculus more understandable, memorable, and engaging. What Is Consciousness? Science Still Has No Answer!
candidates.description: You're reading this right now, and it feels like someone is home inside your head. But what is that feeling? Science still can't fully explain it. 🧠 In this Short, stickmen break down what consciousness actually is, why philosophers call it the "hard problem," what 86 billion neurons can and can't tell us, and why anesthesia makes the mystery even stranger. What you'll learn: 🔴 Consciousness is your inner experience: the redness of red, the sting of a stubbed toe 🧩 The hard problem of consciousness, named by philosopher David Chalmers in 1995 ⚡ The human brain has about 86 billion neurons, yet we still can't explain why their activity feels like anything 💡 Two leading theories: information broadcast across the whole brain (global workspace) vs. how deeply connected information is (integrated information). A 2025 head-to-head test published in Nature supported parts of both and challenged key claims of each, so neither is proven 😴 Anesthesia can switch consciousness off and bring it back, and researchers describe it as a reversible, drug-induced coma, yet exactly how it works is still being studied Sources: 📚 David Chalmers, "Facing Up to the Problem of Consciousness" (1995): https://philpapers.org/rec/CHAFUT 📚 Azevedo et al., "Equal numbers of neuronal and nonneuronal cells make the human brain an isometrically scaled-up primate brain" (2009): https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19226510/ 📚 Cogitate Consortium, "Adversarial testing of global neuronal workspace and integrated information theories of consciousness," Nature (2025): https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-025-08888-1 📚 PubMed record for the same Nature study: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40307561/ 📚 Brown, Lydic & Schiff, "General Anesthesia, Sleep, and Coma" (2010), press summary: https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/747753 📚 Network-level mechanisms of anesthesia and loss of consciousness (review): https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6520142 Subscribe to Stick Animation for more in motion! 🎬 #Consciousness #HardProblemOfConsciousness #Neuroscience #Brain #Philosophy #ScienceMysteries #StickmanAnimation

candidates.description: What is Emotional intelligence is a question about how well we understand and manage emotions—both our own and those of other people. In psychology, emotional intelligence involves recognizing emotions accurately, understanding emotional information, using it to support thinking, and regulating emotions effectively. Emotional intelligence can influence the way we communicate, handle conflicts, build relationships and respond to difficult situations. Important aspects include self-awareness, self-regulation, empathy and social awareness. It does not mean suppressing emotions or never getting angry, sad or anxious; instead, it involves recognizing what you are feeling and responding thoughtfully rather than reacting automatically. candidates.description: Your fingers never really touch your phone…#QuantumPhysics #QuantumMechanics #Physics #Science #Mbbs Have you ever wondered whether you truly touch anything? 🤯 According to quantum physics, touching is more complicated than it seems! Atoms contain nuclei surrounded by electron clouds. When your hand approaches a table, electromagnetic interactions between the atoms resist being pushed together. The Pauli exclusion principle, a fundamental quantum rule, also helps explain why ordinary matter resists compression. Your skin’s sensory receptors detect the resulting pressure and send signals to your brain, creating the sensation of touch. candidates.title: You Have NEVER Actually Touched Anything! 🤯⚛️ #QuantumPhysics #ScientificFacts #SciFlo #science
candidates.description: Have you ever wondered if you have REALLY touched anything in your entire life? 🤯 According to quantum physics, the reality of touch is far stranger than you might imagine! When you touch another person, hold your phone, or place your hand against a wall, the atoms in your body don’t simply collide like tiny solid objects. Instead, something fascinating happens at the atomic level. ⚛️ THE SCIENCE BEHIND TOUCH 1. Atoms: Everything around you, including your body, is made of atoms. 2. Electrons: Atoms contain negatively charged electrons surrounding their nuclei. 3. Electromagnetic Repulsion: When atoms approach one another, electromagnetic interactions between their electrons strongly resist further compression. 4. Pauli Exclusion Principle: This quantum mechanical principle also helps prevent electrons from occupying identical quantum states. 5. The Sensation of Touch: Your nervous system detects forces and pressure through specialized receptors in your skin, allowing your brain to experience the sensation of touching something. 6. The Quantum Reality: What feels like physical contact is actually the result of complex electromagnetic and quantum interactions between matter. So, when you shake someone’s hand, touch a wall, or hold your phone, you’re experiencing forces between atoms rather than tiny solid surfaces simply meeting. IMPORTANT SCIENTIFIC FACT: Saying that you never touch anything is a simplified way of describing atomic interactions. It doesn’t mean physical contact is imaginary or that atoms never interact. candidates.title: The Old Fisherman (1902) – Fold It InHalf And A Demon Shows Up.
candidates.description: The Old Fisherman is a 1902 painting by Tivadar Kosztka Csontváry — a Hungarian artist who painted this calm, weathered fisherman at the end of his life. At first glance it is just a portrait of an old man with a staff, standing against the sea. Then you mirror the canvas down the middle. Take the right half and mirror it: the fisherman is praying, eyes closed, hands at rest. Take the left half and mirror it: the face turns into a horned demon, staring straight back at you. Same paint. Same face. Two completely different people. In this Short we look at the hidden details in this painting — the symmetry trick Csontváry built into the composition, the two faces hiding in one canvas, and why the artist painted it at all. Ink & Instinct is where famous paintings explained meets the strange details nobody points out — art mysteries, symbolism and hidden meanings inside historic artworks. Which half did you see first — the praying man or the demon? Tell me in the comments. 🔔 Subscribe for one art mystery every week. 5 Japanese Phrases for When Something Goes Wrong — and the Numbers to Call
candidates.description: Japan is very safe. These five phrases are the small amount of preparation that stays worth doing anyway. For solo travellers and anyone moving to Japan. Ten seconds of preparation for a situation you will probably never meet. Taught by Saku. ▶ Learn Japanese live, 1-on-1, with a hand-picked teacher: https://kodawari-sensei.com/en?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=social&utm_content=kt31saku ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ 🚨 The five やめてください — yamete kudasai — "Stop it!" たすけてください — tasukete kudasai — "Help me!" だいじょうぶです — daijōbu desu — "No, thank you." / "I'm fine." けいさつをよんでください — keisatsu o yonde kudasai — "Call the police." えいごはなせますか？ — eigo hanasemasu ka? — "Do you speak English?" **110** — police · **119** — fire and ambulance. Both free from any phone, including a locked one. **だいじょうぶです is the one you will actually use** — it is how you decline anything in Japan, firmly and without confrontation. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ 🗾 The small police box on the corner 交番 — こうばん — kōban — a neighbourhood police box 交 — こう — kō — exchange, alternate 番 — ばん — ban — a turn, a watch, a number Literally "alternating watch" — officers took shifts. **There are over 6,000 of them across Japan**, usually a small building at a busy intersection with a red lamp outside, staffed around the clock. **And it is the single most useful thing to know about being lost in Japan.** A 交番 is not a police station — it is closer to a permanently staffed help desk that happens to be police. Officers there will: - give you directions, with a map, at any hour - take lost property. **Japan's lost-and-found rate is genuinely remarkable** and it runs through 交番. - lend you the train fare home in some cases 落とし物 — おとしもの — otoshimono — a lost item 忘れ物 — わすれもの — wasuremono — something left behind 交番はどこですか — kōban wa doko desu ka — where's the police box? **If you lose something on a train**, it goes to the station office first and then to a central lost property centre. Report it — the recovery rate for phones and wallets in Japan is high enough that it is worth the twenty minutes. candidates.title: Möbius Strip Explained: How a 3D Object Has 1 Side
candidates.description: If you trace a line down the center of a Möbius strip, you will cover both apparent faces without ever lifting your pen or crossing an edge. This 10-second visual breaks down how a single 180-degree half-twist transforms an ordinary flat strip into a non-orientable 3D surface. Unlike a standard cylindrical loop—which has two separate sides and two separate edges—a Möbius strip merges everything into one continuous surface and one continuous boundary edge. There is an even stranger geometric consequence: because the surface is non-orientable, traveling one full loop around the strip brings you back to your starting point upside down. It takes two complete loops to return to your exact original orientation. That same geometry has practical engineering value. Industrial conveyor belts designed as Möbius strips distribute friction across the entire surface instead of wearing out only one side, effectively extending the belt's lifespan. Save this Short as a quick visual reference for topology and geometry, or share it with someone who loves counterintuitive math. #MobiusStrip #Topology #MathExplained

candidates.description: Your brain constructs reality rather than recording it passively. candidates.title: How A Wankel Rotary Engine Works⚙️ #physics #automobile #engineering #pixelart #engineeringexplained
candidates.description: *The following figures are for a typical twin-rotor Wankel engine.* Unlike a conventional piston engine, a rotary engine uses triangular rotors spinning inside specially shaped housings to produce power. Each rotor creates three separate chambers, which continuously go through four stages: 1. Intake: Air and fuel enter the chamber. 2. Compression: The mixture is compressed. 3. Combustion: Spark plugs ignite the mixture, pushing the rotor and producing power. 4. Exhaust: The burnt gases are expelled. All four stages happen simultaneously, but in different chambers! And here's the crazy part: 🔥 At 9,000 RPM, a twin-rotor engine produces approximately 300 combustion events per second! 🔥 Even at 1,000 RPM idle, that's around 33 combustion events per second! A fascinating piece of engineering that produces power in a completely different way. *The sound is an illustrative recreation, not an actual recording of a specific car or engine.* **Sources:** - Mazda – Rotary Engine Technical Information - Haynes Manuals – Guide to Rotary Engines - MDPI – Two-Stroke Wankel Type Rotary Engine (2019) #RotaryEngine #Engineering #Automotive #Mechanics #8BitEngineering

candidates.title: How to Build a Tank, One Problem at a Time 🪖 #shorts
candidates.description: Bolt steel plates onto a farm tractor and you are one problem away from the next part. Mud, trenches, a gun that only points one way, an engine that cooks the crew, no radio, and tea. Every part of a tank exists because something went wrong first. Why are tracks called caterpillar tracks? Why was the first tank shaped like a rhombus? Why do British tanks have a kettle built in? And why is it called a "tank" at all? Facts in this short: • The British Army asked for a machine that could cross a trench 8 feet wide. That is why the first tanks (1916) had tracks running all the way around a rhomboid hull. • Inside the Mark I the crew shared one space with the engine: up to 122 °F (50 °C), exhaust fumes, and men passing out. • The Renault FT (1917) put the gun in a fully rotating turret and the engine in its own compartment at the back. Almost every tank since has copied that layout. • Early tanks had no radio. Crews carried two carrier pigeons. • Since the Centurion (1945), British tanks carry a built-in boiling vessel for hot water, rations and tea. • In 1915 the secret machines were described as "water carriers for Mesopotamia". The code name stuck: tank. #engineering #tank #history #howitworks #ww1 #science #shorts

candidates.title: How One Tiny Cap Beat Sloped Armor
candidates.description: Why did tank shells bounce off sloped armor, and how did engineers fix it? 💥 Early armor-piercing shells had pointed noses. When they hit angled armor, they often glanced off or shattered. The fix was a blunt armor-piercing cap that bites into the plate and makes the shell far less likely to ricochet. A blunt nose is bad for aerodynamics, though, so a thin, hollow ballistic cap went on top. It made the shell sleek in flight and crumpled on impact, so the blunt cap underneath could do its job. The result was the APCBC round: Armor-Piercing, Capped, Ballistic Capped. 🎯 Would you have guessed the pointy tip was fake? 👇 📌 Cutaway reference: Blockhaj, "APCBC-HE-T example," Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA) #Shorts #TankHistory #APCBC #WW2 #MilitaryHistory #Armor #3DAnimation #Engineering Understand how things work with Unfold. candidates.title: Run or Attack? How Ancient Tribes Handled Strangers  #humanhistory
candidates.description: Imagine you spot smoke from a group of strangers you've never met. Run, or attack? It turns out there was a third option, and it was far smarter. Anthropologist Polly Wiessner studied the Ju/'hoansi people of the Kalahari Desert. They have a tradition called hxaro: trading gifts with groups who live far away. What you're really buying is trust, because when a drought hits, your hxaro partner will open their land to you. This pattern is very old. About 320,000 years ago at Olorgesailie in Kenya, a team led by Alan Brooks found obsidian from a source almost a hundred kilometers away, which may have arrived through trade between groups. Humans didn't survive by being the fiercest. They survived by turning strangers into friends. What would you trade if you met a group of strangers? Tell us in the comments. Sources: - Polly Wiessner (hxaro, Ju/'hoansi, Kalahari Desert) - Alan Brooks (Olorgesailie obsidian, Kenya) #AncientHumans #HumanHistory #Anthropology

How much? — いくらですか？ (Ikura desu ka?) 7. Where is...? — どこですか？ (Doko desu ka?) 8. Please — おねがいします (Onegaishimasu) 9. I'm sorry — ごめんなさい (Gomen nasai) 10. Goodbye — さようなら (Sayounara) ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ 🗾 The question that works in any shop ありますか — arimasu ka — do you have it? ある is the verb for something existing, used for objects rather than people. Point at anything, or name it, add ありますか, and the question is complete. candidates.title: Ockham’s Razor — The Power of Simplicity

channel.name: Undying Truths And Facts of Life

candidates.description: Description What if the secret to scientific discovery is not adding more explanations, but knowing which ones we can do without? In this episode of UTFL SCI-PHI (Science Meets Philosophy), we explore Ockham’s Razor, a powerful principle associated with the medieval philosopher William of Ockham. Its central message is simple: do not multiply assumptions beyond necessity. From the transformation of astronomy to Newton’s universal gravitation and modern scientific research, discover why scientists often seek explanations that are simple, powerful, and consistent with the evidence. But does the simplest explanation always turn out to be true? Not necessarily! Nature can be complex, and a beautiful theory is not enough unless it survives scientific testing. This short cinematic journey explores the relationship between simplicity, evidence, critical thinking, and scientific progress. It also reveals an important lesson: philosophy helps us examine our assumptions, while science tests our explanations against reality. The SCI-PHI takeaway: Seek the simplest explanation that adequately fits the facts, but never sacrifice evidence for simplicity. Welcome to UTFL, where science meets philosophy to help us understand the world and ourselves. Subscribe for more cinematic stories exploring science, philosophy, nature, and the undying truths and facts of life. UTFL SCI-PHI: Speak the Truth. candidates.description: 🏹 WHAT HAPPENS TO YOUR PROJECT WHEN THE LEADER IS AWAY? Does work continue smoothly—or do important decisions pile up? The story of Bharata's Padukas from the Ramayana offers a powerful lesson about delegation, authority, and responsible leadership. Welcome to Episode 02 of Ramayana × Project Management by PMO Wisdom! 🎯 TODAY'S STORY: BHARATA'S PADUKAS When Rama was in exile, Bharata placed Rama's sandals (Padukas) on the throne and governed in his name for fourteen years. Bharata's actions symbolised his commitment to Rama's rightful authority and his responsibility to serve as a steward. What can project managers learn from this story? ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ 📘 LESSON 1: MAKE AUTHORITY VISIBLE ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ Everyone should know who has the authority to make decisions. In project management, unclear decision rights can create delays, confusion, and unnecessary escalation. Before a planned absence, clarify: ✅ Who can make routine decisions ✅ Which decisions require escalation ✅ What approval limits apply ✅ Who communicates important decisions A project should not stop simply because one person is unavailable. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ 📘 LESSON 2: ACT AS A STEWARD, NOT AN OWNER ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ Bharata governed in Rama's name rather than claiming the throne as his own. In project management, delegated authority should be exercised responsibly. A project manager or deputy should: • Respect the sponsor's intent • Work within agreed decision limits • Protect the project's objectives • Remain accountable for decisions made Leadership is about serving the agreed purpose, not treating delegated authority as personal power. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ 📘 LESSON 3: HAND BACK CLEANLY ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ Delegation should include a clear process for handing responsibility back. Maintain: ✅ A transparent decision log ✅ Records of important approvals ✅ A list of unresolved issues ✅ Clear communication about changes When the original leader returns, they should be able to understand what happened and resume responsibility without confusion. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ 💡 PRACTICAL PROJECT EXAMPLE ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ Imagine a project manager takes three weeks of leave. It is the clarity of delegated authority. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ ⚠️ MISTAKE TO AVOID ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ Leaving a project without clear delegation. When nobody knows who can decide, even small issues may remain unresolved. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ 🎯 TRY THIS IN YOUR NEXT PROJECT ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ Before your next planned absence: 1️⃣ Identify your deputy. 2️⃣ Define their decision-making authority. 3️⃣ Agree on escalation limits. 4️⃣ Establish a decision log and handback process. candidates.title: Your Brain Is Not Creating Your Consciousness? (Theory #2)
candidates.description: Is your brain the source of consciousness, or just the receiver? Most neuroscientists hold a materialist view: consciousness is produced by the brain, so when the brain stops, consciousness ends. But a minority of researchers propose the opposite. In this view, consciousness is non-local: it is not created by neurons but filtered, tuned and transmitted through the brain, the way a radio or a television picks up a signal broadcast from somewhere else. Smash the radio, and the music stops. But does that mean the station is gone? In this Short we explore the two sides of one of the biggest open questions in science and philosophy. THE TWO VIEWS • Materialism: consciousness is an emergent product of brain activity. No brain activity, no consciousness. • Non-local consciousness (the "transmission" or "filter" theory): the brain is a receiver, not the source. Some proponents go further and describe consciousness as fundamental, non-physical, even eternal, and some link it to quantum ideas or to what many traditions call God or the Divine. These are philosophical and speculative claims, not proven science. WHO IS EXPLORING THIS? • William James, the philosopher and psychologist, suggested over a century ago that the brain might transmit consciousness instead of producing it. • Dr. Pim van Lommel, a Dutch cardiologist, studied hundreds of cardiac arrest survivors and argues that vivid experiences during a failing brain challenge the brain-only view. • Dr. Eben Alexander, a neurosurgeon, claims his neocortex was offline during a seven-day coma, yet he remembers an intense experience. His case is disputed by critics. • Dr. Bruce Greyson, the late Dr. Peter Fenwick, and Dr. Edward Kelly's team at the University of Virginia continue to investigate. IS IT PROVEN? No. Skeptics argue that a dying brain can still generate these experiences, and that no experiment has yet shown consciousness existing without a functioning brain. Defenders of the non-local view argue that the materialist model cannot explain why anything is experienced at all (the "hard problem of consciousness"). The question is still open, and what is at stake is nothing less than what we are. What do you think: is the brain the source of consciousness, or the receiver? Tell us in the comments. Follow for more on near-death experiences and the true nature of consciousness. #consciousness #neardeathexperience #nde #brain #science #nonlocalconsciousness #shorts

candidates.title: The 10,000 Steps Rule Came From a Product Name #anthropology #animation #cartoon #motivation #fan
candidates.description: In 1965 a Japanese company called Yamasa put a small clip-on step counter on the market. They named it Manpo-Kei — "ten thousand steps meter" — and sold it with the slogan "let's walk ten thousand steps a day." That is where the number comes from. Not a study. A product name. Sixty years later it sits inside your watch, your phone and your insurance app, and it still feels like medicine. Researchers have since measured walking properly, and the benefits do not switch on at exactly ten thousand. The number was never wrong. It was just never measured. candidates.title: How a Bike Chain Reduces Your Effort ⚙️ 3 Chain Systems Explained #shorts
candidates.description: 3 bikes. 3 chain systems. Here's the engineering that makes pedalling easier 👇 ⚙️ 01 · Two-stage chain drive Chainring → jackshaft → rear sprocket. The load is split across two short chains, and the jackshaft near the swing-arm pivot keeps chain length almost constant as the suspension moves, so there's minimal pedal kickback. Overall ratio: i = i1 × i2 ⚙️ 02 · Cassette + chain tensioner An idler keeps the chain line stable, and a spring-loaded cage keeps tension constant on every cog. Wheel torque = crank torque × (rear cog ÷ chainring), so a bigger cog means a lower gear and an easier climb. Roller links roll onto the teeth instead of sliding, for up to ~98% efficiency. ⚙️ 03 · Mid-drive e-bike drivetrain A narrow-wide chainring holds the chain without a front derailleur. The motor's torque goes through the crank, so the gears multiply it too. A derailleur bolted straight to the axle stays rigidly aligned, and the 10–52T cassette gives a 520% range. Less effort = right ratio × high efficiency × constant tension. 👍 Like if you learned something 🔔 Subscribe for more engineering explained #shorts #bike #mtb #ebike #engineering #mechanicalengineering #cycling #bikemechanic #drivetrain #gears

candidates.title: Einstein Was Wrong About Quantum Mechanics
candidates.description: Can two particles on opposite ends of the universe affect each other instantly? Albert Einstein called it "spooky action at a distance" and insisted hidden variables must exist—like a matching pair of socks in two boxes. In 1964, physicist John Bell devised an equation to test this once and for all. candidates.title: How We Think in Containers #wuwei #overthinking #alanwatts #cognitivescience #philosophy
candidates.description: How does your brain process an invisible concept like "falling in love" or "getting out of debt"? We never evolved dedicated biological hardware for abstract philosophy. Instead, human cognition pulls off a mechanical cheat called metaphorical projection. Your baseline understanding of reality is anchored in embodied motor interaction: • The Container Logic: Stepping physically across the boundary of an enclosed space gives you the spatial rules for "inside" and "outside." Because emotional states don't have physical drywall, your neural circuits recycle container logic to "enter an agreement" or "get out of a rut." • The Gravitational Axis: You spend every waking second fighting gravity to remain upright. Your motor cortex maps upward stability to high-energy emotional states ("cheering up," "rising to the occasion") and downward collapse to low-energy states ("feeling down," "falling into depression"). All higher-level human meaning is grounded in the physical chassis moving through three-dimensional space. The next time you "climb out of trouble," your brain isn't running abstract computations—it is literally navigating an imaginary box. Master the physical vehicle. Understand the cognitive map. candidates.title: Avoid This Rookie Public Speaking Mistake
candidates.description: Want to own the stage without pacing it? Comment STRESSFREE and my free presentation training is yours. Pacing the stage tells the room you are nervous. You have seen this speaker. They never stand still. They wander from one side to the other, often looking down at the floor as they go. In the video I explain what that movement is really telling the audience. Constant wandering signals that you are not comfortable standing behind what you are saying. The audience may not put it into words, but they feel it. The message sounds less certain because the body delivering it will not settle, however strong the words are. That does not mean you have to freeze. Movement is fine. But move with purpose. Walk towards the audience, or the camera, to make a point land. Then, once you get there, stop. Plant your feet. Present. Stillness is where your gestures do their best work. Planted feet give your hands a stable base, and every movement you make from there looks deliberate rather than nervous. Move, stop, plant, present. Practise that rhythm and you will look like you own the stage instead of searching for somewhere to hide on it. The audience relaxes when you do. Do you tend to wander when you speak, or freeze on the spot? #PublicSpeaking #StagePresence #Gestures #BodyLanguage #Confidence

candidates.title: Who Invented the Rolling Suitcase (1970)
candidates.description: TITLE: Who Invented the Rolling Suitcase (1970) SHORT COVER / THUMBNAIL TEXT (3 words max, optional): NOT FOR MEN DESCRIPTION: Bernard Sadow invented the rolling suitcase in 1970 after bolting four furniture wheels onto a bag with a pull-strap. Here is why department stores laughed and suitcases had no wheels until 1970—until Macy's sold "The Luggage That Glides." Humanity had already landed on the Moon in 1969, yet air travelers were still hauling heavy bags by hand. After struggling through airport customs with two massive suitcases and spotting a worker rolling a heavy machine on four wheels, Bernard Sadow built a wheeled suitcase that same night and walked it through New York on a leash. Buyers laughed him out of stores with "No real man is rolling his bag" until he bypassed the buyer and rolled his prototype straight into a Macy's vice president's office. By October 1970, Macy's put it on display as "The Luggage That Glides"—and two years after U.S. Patent #3,653,474 was granted, rival luggage companies banded together in court trying to break it so they could copy it. candidates.title: BrahMos: Mach 3 Cruise Missile!
candidates.description: BrahMos is one of the fastest cruise missiles in operation, flying at about three times the speed of sound. In this short Hindi-narrated video, we explain how this India-Russia missile works, in simple words and without the hype. BrahMos is a joint India-Russia project, and it can be launched from land, ships, submarines or aircraft. It flies at about Mach 2.8 to 3, which is around 3,700 km/h. What you will learn: • Why BrahMos is counted among the fastest operational cruise missiles • How the India-Russia project works, and from which platforms it can be launched • The warhead: officially conventional, about 200 kg, and up to 300 kg in the air-launched version • The two stages: a solid booster takes it to supersonic speed and separates, then a liquid ramjet engine keeps it near Mach 3 • The flight path: it can fly high, up to about 15 km, and drop to as low as about 5 metres at the end, which makes it harder to detect • The "fire and forget" idea, and the range: about 290 km for the standard version, with newer versions reported at 450 km or more Extra context beyond the video: • Some websites claim BrahMos can carry a nuclear warhead. The official BrahMos site describes a conventional warhead, so we do not make that claim • "World's fastest" depends on how you define the category, so we say "one of the fastest operational cruise missiles" • Range figures vary by version and by report • This video is an educational explainer. We have not added technical details beyond what is publicly available • Based on official BrahMos information and defence reporting, current as of November 24, 2026 Facts, not hype. candidates.title: Waking the Brain: Does Consciousness Have a Dial?
candidates.description: After a severe brain injury, some people survive but never fully come back. They may open their eyes yet show little or no sign of awareness, sometimes for years. Doctors have a strong suspect: the thalamus, a hub deep in the center of the brain that helps keep the rest of it switched on. After injury it often goes quiet. Surgeons have tried to reach it with implanted electrodes. At UCLA, Martin Monti's team tried sound. A device about the size of a saucer, held against the side of the head, focused low-intensity ultrasound onto the thalamus. They reported on three people who had lived with a disorder of consciousness for more than a year. Two changed. A 56-year-old man, more than 14 months after a stroke, could then grasp a ball when asked and nod yes or no. A 50-year-old woman, more than two and a half years after cardiac arrest, could then recognise objects. The third patient did not change. The limits are large. Three patients. No placebo group. Small changes. No sham-controlled result has been published yet, so this is far from proven. For a family, even one answered question can mean the world. For science, it is a hint that consciousness may have a dial, deep in the brain. Source: Cain et al., Brain Stimulation, 2021, as described in UCLA's release. A science explainer, not medical advice. candidates.description: Turn an electron all the way around, one full turn, and it's not back where it started. You have to turn it twice. In under 3 minutes: 1922: Otto Stern and Walther Gerlach fire silver atoms through a specially shaped magnet. Instead of one long stripe, they land in just two spots: up or down 1925: George Uhlenbeck and Samuel Goudsmit propose the electron spins like a tiny planet, making it a tiny magnet But it can't literally spin: its surface would have to move more than 100 times faster than light, and the electron has no measurable size at all Spin is a built-in twist the electron simply has. Physicists call it angular momentum, always exactly the same amount Turn an electron 360° and its quantum wave flips upside down. candidates.title: What's Really Under Antarctica's Ice?

In the east, the Gamburtsev Mountains rise nearly 3 km high, buried so deep not a single peak breaks the surface. Beside them lies Lake Vostok, a liquid lake 250 km long, sealed in total darkness for millions of years. And under Denman Glacier, the land plunges 3,500 m below sea level, 8x deeper than the Dead Sea and the deepest land on Earth. All that ice holds about 70% of Earth's fresh water. If it melted, global sea level would rise around 58 metres. 📊 Data: Terrain from NOAA ETOPO 2022 (BedMachine Antarctica under the ice). Heights exaggerated ×25 so you can see them. candidates.title: Countries that almost touch (not Russia and the USA)  #facts #shorts
candidates.description: Of all the countries that almost touch, Namibia and Zimbabwe are the closest, less than 200 m apart, while Russia and the USA are only #7. The closest countries that don't share a border (every island counts): 1 Namibia–Zimbabwe 178 m, 2 Grenada–St Vincent and the Grenadines 710 m, 3 Bahrain–Qatar 744 m, 4 UK–USA about 1 km (British and US Virgin Islands), 5 Malaysia–Singapore about 1 km (Straits of Johor), 6 Malaysia–Philippines 1.9 km, 7 Russia–USA 3.8 km (the Diomede Islands, "Tomorrow Island" and "Yesterday Island"). Between Namibia and Zimbabwe, at Kazungula, sits the tiny 150 m border of Botswana and Zambia. Bahrain's Hawar Island is closer to Qatar than to the rest of Bahrain. Many older maps (Natural Earth too) draw Kazungula as one point where four countries meet; they don't. Rule: UN member states with no land border (CIA World Factbook, final edition), measured between the nearest land each holds today, islands and overseas territories included; bridges, causeways and disputed land don't count. Measured on OpenStreetMap; sources differ by a few hundred metres for the closest pairs (Bahrain–Qatar is about 1.85 km on Wikipedia). Why not… Greece–Turkey, Spain–Morocco (Ceuta, Melilla), France–Netherlands (Saint Martin) and Canada–Denmark (Hans Island, since 2022) all share a land border, so they aren't gaps. Japan–Russia (3.7 km) is disputed land, so it's left out. #shorts #geography #countries #maps #borders #unitedstates

candidates.title: Are Microtubules the Seat of Consciousness?
candidates.description: Most biologists look at microtubules and see scaffolding. A few researchers see the mind. Microtubules are tubes about 25 nanometers across that run through every neuron. They give the cell its shape and carry cargo along their length. In the Orch-OR theory of Stuart Hameroff and Roger Penrose, they do something more. The theory says each tubulin protein in the tube can sit in superposition, two shapes at once, and act as a quantum bit. If those bits were orchestrated across a neuron, Hameroff argues, it could explain what computer models of the mind struggle with: why experience feels unified, and why it feels like anything at all. The big objection is heat and noise. In warm, living tissue, critics calculate that quantum states would fall apart far too fast. Supporters answer that the microtubule's geometry, and ordered water inside the tube, might protect them for longer. That has not been shown in a living brain. Terahertz measurements and anesthetic studies have kept the debate alive without settling it. This is a minority view. Source: the Orch-OR theory of Stuart Hameroff and Roger Penrose. A science explainer about a hypothesis, not established science. A science short from UltraDAO · ultradao.to #neuroscience #consciousness #quantumbiology #microtubules #sciencecommunication

candidates.title: The Impossible Calculation Holding the Universe Together #space #physics #cosmology
candidates.description: According to quantum mechanics, empty space isn't actually empty—it boils with unseen virtual particles producing an immense repulsive energy that pushes the cosmos apart. When physicists calculated how much of this vacuum energy fills our universe, their prediction missed by a factor of 10¹²⁰—a one followed by 120 zeros. It remains the largest error in the history of science. Yet if that original calculation had been right, the universe would have expanded so violently that stars, planets, and atoms never would have formed. For reality to survive, the opposing positive and negative energies of the cosmos must cancel each other out down to the 120th decimal place. Does this knife-edge calibration point to an infinite multiverse of dead universes, or was reality fine-tuned on purpose? #space #physics #cosmology

candidates.title: Why Is This Country Stuck Inside Senegal? 🌍 #geography #facts #shorts
candidates.description: Gambia is a sliver of land surrounded by Senegal, defined entirely by the path of the Gambia River. This geography is the result of 19th-century colonial rivalry, where British and French interests fought for control over the river and the surrounding territory. The country acts as a narrow corridor cutting into Senegal, a shape dictated by how far upriver naval vessels could effectively patrol and claim land during that era. Understanding the Gambia River explains why the nation exists as an enclave today. The border follows the riverbanks, leaving the country isolated within its larger neighbor. This unique political geography demonstrates how historical claims by European empires permanently altered the map of Africa. candidates.description: Play this V8 + get its full soundtrack → link in bio 🎮🎧 A V8 fires a bang every quarter turn, perfectly evenly. But its crank is a cross, so each side's exhaust gets its 4 bangs unevenly. Two pipes, two lopsided rhythms: that IS the rumble. (A flat-plane crank alternates the sides evenly, and the rumble's gone.) 🎮 V8 LAB: swap the firing order, flip the crank, hear the beat change, rev it till it breaks 🎧 THE FULL V8 SOUNDTRACK: this beat, 2 minutes long 👉 Both at the link in bio · 8bitengineering.org 📚 SOURCES • Firing order 1-8-4-3-6-5-7-2 + the 350's 101.6 × 88.4 mm bore and stroke: Wikipedia, "Chevrolet small-block engine (1954–2003)" • Cross-plane crank, even firing overall but uneven on each bank: Wikipedia, "Crossplane" • Uneven pulses on each bank = the V8 rumble: Toyota Times, "Behind the Engine Tones that are Music to the Ears of Car Lovers" · Car Throttle, "Why Do Different Engine Configurations Make Different Sounds?" · BBC Science Focus, "Why do V8 engines sound so good?" • Braps = unburnt fuel going off in the hot exhaust: Wikipedia, "Back-fire" • 55 bangs a second at idle: 825 rpm ÷ 60 × 4 = 55 ⚠️ HEADS UP No real engine recordings in this video. Every engine sound is synthesized from the animation's own crank, so sound and picture stay locked together, even in slow-mo. Real V8 recordings were only a tone reference; none of their audio is in here. The slow-mo bangs are designed sounds, and the beat is original. The engine is a simplified illustration (a generic cross-plane V8 with the small-block Chevy's firing order), and the revs and pops are timed to the beat. candidates.title: Orch-OR in 90 Seconds: Is Consciousness a Quantum Event?
candidates.description: What if consciousness isn't only neurons firing, but quantum events inside the cell's skeleton? That is the idea behind Orchestrated Objective Reduction, or Orch-OR, from anesthesiologist Stuart Hameroff and physicist Roger Penrose. Every neuron is threaded with microtubules: hollow tubes built from a protein called tubulin. The theory puts the action there. In Orch-OR, tubulin proteins enter quantum superposition. When enough of them are entangled, gravity collapses the state. Penrose calls that collapse objective reduction. Each collapse would be one moment of awareness, so experience would arrive as a series of ticks, not as continuous computation. Now the limits. Most scientists remain skeptical. The brain is warm, wet and noisy, and critics argue quantum states there would fall apart far too fast to matter. Supporters point to experiments suggesting microtubules can carry coherent vibrations, and to anesthetics that bind tubulin. Neither settles it. As of 2026, Orch-OR is still a hypothesis. But the idea keeps generating experiments. Source: the Orch-OR theory of Stuart Hameroff and Roger Penrose. A science explainer about a hypothesis, not established science. A science short from UltraDAO · ultradao.to #neuroscience #consciousness #quantumbiology #microtubules #sciencecommunication

The short ones find the detail most people miss in a famous painting; the long ones pair paintings with classical music for reading, studying or a quiet evening. Claude Monet painted the harbour of Le Havre at sunrise in 1872, and the picture gave Impressionism its name. The orange sun looks like the brightest thing on the canvas, but when its brightness is measured, it is the same as the grey sky around it. Take the colour away and the sun almost disappears. Harvard neuroscientist Margaret Livingstone explains why it seems to shimmer: the part of our vision that judges position and depth sees only brightness, not colour, so it can't pin the sun down. candidates.title: Why a Coffee Cup and a Donut Are the Same Shape (Topology Explained)
candidates.description: To a mathematician, a coffee cup and a donut are the same shape. ☕🍩 This is topology, the study of properties that stay the same when you stretch, bend, or squeeze an object without tearing or gluing. A mug has one handle-like hole going all the way through it, and so does a donut. Squish the cup’s bowl down, grow the handle, and you get a donut, with no cutting required. Mathematicians say the two are homeomorphic, and both have genus 1. A sphere is different. It has no through-hole, so you can’t turn it into a donut without tearing a hole in it. 🔴 Topology ignores size, thickness, and curvature and focuses on the underlying structure that links seemingly different shapes. In this short, you’ll learn: ✅ What topology studies ✅ What a through-hole and genus are ✅ What homeomorphic means ✅ Why a sphere can’t become a donut without tearing 👍 Like if this changed how you see your coffee cup 💬 Comment: What everyday object would you try next, a pretzel, a pair of glasses, or a bowl? 🔔 Subscribe for more math, physics, and chemistry explained clearly ↗️ Share with someone who loves puzzles or math #Shorts #Topology #Math #Mathematics #Donut #CoffeeCup #Geometry #STEM #MathExplained #ScienceExplained

candidates.title: Why Achilles can never catch the tortoise (Zeno's paradox) #shorts
candidates.description: The fastest runner in Greece can never catch a tortoise. Here's the argument. Give the tortoise a head start. By the time Achilles reaches where it was, it has moved on a little. He reaches that spot, and it has moved again. Forever. So how does he ever get past? Zeno of Elea said the same about any walk: first half the way, then half of what's left, endlessly. The modern answer is a convergent series: 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + … adds up to exactly 1. Infinitely many steps, one finite distance. (In the Short's example, a 100 m head start against a runner 10× faster: 100 + 10 + 1 + 0.1 + … = 111.1… m.) Mathematics gives a clean answer. Whether it ends the argument is still debated. Did math settle it? Tell us in the comments. Zeno is one stop on the road from philosophy to physics. The full story is in the main video: https://youtu.be/InA0X4OyxQo More: https://www.youtube.com/@atoms_and_awe Sources • Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Zeno's Paradoxes" (the dichotomy and Achilles; replies by Russell, Grünbaum, Salmon): https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/paradox-zeno/ • Aristotle, Physics VI.9, 239b14 (Achilles) Visuals: our own illustrations. candidates.title: A Message Is Only as Good as Its Delivery #communication #emotionalintelligence
candidates.description: A Message Is Only as Good as Its Delivery. Something can seem obvious to us and still be confusing to someone else. The way we respond can make them comfortable asking another question or embarrassed to admit they’re lost. That matters, because a nod doesn’t always mean the message got through. Helping someone understand takes patience, but also a willingness to explain things differently instead of expecting everyone to think like us. Before getting frustrated that someone doesn’t understand, it’s worth asking: have we explained it in a way that makes sense to them?
